name: Approval of September 17, 1859 of the La Pointe band's Madeline Island reserve
citation: Secretary of the Interior's approval of selections, under Article 2 (second clause) of the Treaty with the Chippewa, 1854, 10 Stat. 1109
nations: La Pointe band of Lake Superior Ojibwe (Chippewa)
promises: Treaty of September 30, 1854, Article 2, second clause: for the La Pointe band, besides the reserve on the south shore, two hundred acres on the northern extremity of Madeline Island for a fishing ground.
Article 2 opening: the United States agreed to set apart and withhold these tracts from sale for the use of the Chippewa of Lake Superior.
Article 3: the United States to survey the reserves when necessary and to change boundaries only as needed to protect vested rights.
landTaken: This act took no land. Royce records that the Secretary of the Interior approved and reported to the General Land Office the selections for the La Pointe band's reserve on Madeline Island under the 1854 treaty (Royce area 335, Wisconsin).
compensation: Not applicable. In Docket 18-U the Indian Claims Commission counted the Madeline Island reserve, at its January 10, 1855 value, among seven reserves credited to the United States as consideration for the 1854 cession (41 Ind. Cl. Comm. 249, 1978); that finding concerns the 1854 treaty (kappler-656).
today: What became of the Madeline Island reserve after 1859 was not traced in this pass.

nationVoice.nation: Red Cliff Band of Lake Superior Chippewa
nationVoice.summary: The Band, originally part of the La Pointe Band, says Madeline Island (Moo-ning-wana-kawn-ing) was the last stop of the Anishinaabe migration, that Chief Great Buffalo and other chiefs challenged earlier treaties as made by deception and travelled to Washington to meet President Fillmore, who rescinded the removal orders and agreed the Ojibwe would never have to leave their homelands, and that the Treaty of 1854 ceded the largest amount of land.

openQuestions: For Jordan: this entry is not a cession. It is the approval of a reserve promised by the 1854 treaty. treaties.json names it 'Cession of land of the Chippewa of the Mississippi and Lake Superior'; the band concerned was the La Pointe band, whose successors are the Bad River and Red Cliff bands.
Royce's schedule labels the action 'Executive order' but describes it as the Secretary of the Interior's approval; the original document was not opened.
Whether the Madeline Island reserve was later sold, allotted or lost, and whether any finding covers it, was not researched. The Bad River and Red Cliff bands' own accounts are the place to start.
